reason: This was the line most likely to break, because Article I circulates in at least two English renderings and the wrong one is everywhere: the version reading Woman is born free and lives equal to man in her rights is widely attached to Hunt in error. So the named edition was opened rather than trusted. The Liberty, Equality, Fraternity archive page was fetched and the markup stripped, and it prints: Woman is born free and remains equal to man in rights. Social distinctions may be based only on common utility. That is the proposed wording to the letter, and the page carries the credit line translated, edited, and with an introduction by Lynn Hunt (Boston/New York Bedford/St. Martin, 1996), 124 to 129, which matches the edition line as given, page range included. Locator: Article I is the first numbered article after the preamble that ends in the following rights of woman and the citizeness, and the quoted sentence is its first sentence, with the common utility sentence second. Correct. Attribution: the Declaration is de Gouges, September 1791, and no rival claim exists; nothing in the misattribution list touches it. Scope: a pamphlet of 1791, not scripture, not a speech, nothing needing a warning. Cap and shipped: olympe de gouges at 0 of 3, not banned, nothing shipped and no near opening. Source line: 114 characters, leads with the name, no dash, and it names the translator and the year of the translation whose wording it uses, as rule 4 requires of a translated line. Two soft points, neither fatal. First, the archive heads the document simply as The Declaration of the Rights of Woman, so the longer and of the Female Citizen in the source line is the conventional English title rather than the heading the named edition prints; it is the standard title of the work and no reader is misled, but an editor who wants the edition wording can shorten it to The Declaration of the Rights of Woman, September 1791, Article I. Second, the tag Philosophy is the least bad fit in a closed vocabulary that has no place for a declaration, and Essay would be worse. Theme: born free and equal in rights is the September line about what is owed, and it lifts at six in the morning.
